She had called the clinic on a Tuesday afternoon, her hands shaking as she dialed, uncertain whether she was reaching out or simply going through the motions of something she didn't deserve.

Vinh's Story

Vinh Nguyen was forty years old when he finally made the appointment, though he had been carrying the weight of what happened for nearly a decade. He was a journalist then, in 2015, working for an independent news outlet in Southeast Asia, investigating corruption in local government. He had built a reputation for meticulous reporting and fearless questions-the kind of reporter editors trusted with sensitive stories. That reputation had made him a target.

The abduction happened on a Tuesday evening. He was leaving his office when three men in plain clothes forced him into a van. What followed occupied a space in his mind that he could not fully access. He remembered the smell of diesel fuel and the sound of a door slamming, remembered being in a concrete room with a single window high on the wall. But the hours in between-the specific words spoken, the exact sequence of what was done to him-remained fragmented, like a film with missing frames. When he tried to reconstruct it deliberately, the details scattered. What he could not forget, paradoxically, was the feeling: the absolute certainty that he would not leave that room alive, that his body was no longer his own, that the person he had been before walking out of his office no longer existed.

He was released after seventy-two hours. His captors never explained why. He was never formally charged with anything. He returned to his apartment in Hanoi, filed a police report that went nowhere, and tried to resume his work. But something had fractured inside him that did not repair.

Within weeks, Vinh noticed that ordinary sounds made him flinch violently-a car horn, a door slamming, even the neighbor's television through the wall. His body responded to these sounds as though they were threats, flooding him with adrenaline before his mind could catch up. He began eating less, not consciously at first but as a kind of drift. Food tasted like nothing. His mouth felt dry. Eating felt like an act that belonged to a person with a future, and he was no longer certain he had one. Over months, he lost fifteen pounds.

He stopped answering calls from colleagues. A former friend from university, someone named Minh, had texted him to meet for coffee; Vinh deleted the message without responding. The thought of sitting across from someone who knew him before-who could see in his face what had been done to him-was unbearable. He had come to believe that his torture was written on his skin, visible to anyone who looked closely enough. More than that, he was certain there was something fundamentally broken in him now, something that made him unworthy of friendship or ordinary human connection.

The memory of his captivity haunted him precisely because he could not fully remember it. He would lie awake at night trying to reconstruct the sequence, trying to understand what he might have done differently, how he might have prevented this. If he had left the office five minutes earlier. If he had taken a different route. If he had been more careful, more aware, more vigilant. The rumination was exhausting and futile, but he could not stop. The gaps in his memory felt obscene-as though his mind was protecting him from something so terrible that consciousness itself rejected it.

Vinh eventually left journalism. He moved to the United States on a visa, telling himself it was a fresh start. He found work as a freelance translator, a job he could do from home, alone. He lived in Portland now, in a small apartment, and had been there for five years. He watched people closely when he had to go out-the grocery store, the pharmacy-scanning faces for signs of danger, trying to anticipate threats before they materialized. He had never told anyone in America what happened. The secret sat in his chest like a stone.

What brought him finally to seek help was a child crying in the apartment above his. The sound-high-pitched, sustained, utterly ordinary-had sent him into a panic so severe that he could not breathe. He sat on his kitchen floor for two hours, trembling, unable to move. The next morning, he searched for a trauma therapist and made an appointment. He was afraid of what remembering might cost him. He was also afraid of what forgetting had already cost.

Aroha was twenty-three years old when the bombing happened. She had been in the lobby of the Civic Centre in downtown Auckland, waiting for her dance partner to finish a meeting upstairs so they could head to rehearsal together. The foyer was all glass and steel, morning light pouring through the tall windows, and she was standing near the information desk scrolling through her phone when the blast came. The sound was not like anything she had ever heard-not a bang but a compression, a force that seemed to come from inside her own chest first, then from everywhere at once. The windows fractured into a thousand pieces. People fell. She fell. When she tried to move, she could not tell if her leg was pinned or if she simply could not remember how to make her body work. She had survived with relatively minor injuries-a fractured fibula, lacerations on her arms and face-but in the months that followed, the physical wounds became almost incidental to something else that had taken root in her mind.

Now, at twenty-nine, Aroha had been living in a state of fractured existence for six years. The attack had been claimed by a group whose name she heard repeatedly in the news, in conversations, in the careful condolences of friends and family members who would begin sentences and then stop themselves, uncertain whether speaking the name aloud would harm her further. Each time she heard it, her body reacted as though the blast were happening again-her heart would accelerate, her breathing would shallow, and she would find herself gripping whatever was nearest to her. The memories of that morning did not come to her as a coherent sequence but as disconnected sensations and images that refused to assemble into a narrative she could tell. She could recall the angle of light through the windows. She could recall the sound, though the sound itself seemed to exist outside of language-it was not a memory she could describe to another person so much as a physical state she inhabited when it returned to her. Sometimes, lying in bed at night, the full emotional weight of the event would crash through her without any accompanying image, and she would lie rigid, drenched in fear, unable to articulate what she was afraid of in that particular moment. The memories came to her unbidden-fragmentary, sensory, stripped of any sequence that might allow her to contain them. What occupied her mind with increasing frequency, though, was a question that had no answer: why her? Why had she been in that lobby at that exact moment? She had replayed the decision a thousand times-the text from her partner saying the meeting was running late, her choice to wait downstairs rather than go back to the car, the small delay that meant she was standing by the information desk instead of anywhere else. She had come to believe that there must be some reason the event had happened to her specifically, some thread of causality or fate that connected her presence in that place to the violence itself. The not-knowing gnawed at her. Sometimes she wondered if she had done something in her life before the bombing that had warranted this-if there was some moral accounting she had failed to settle. Other times she thought about the bombers themselves, imagining their reasons, their certainties, trying to locate in their ideology some logic that might explain why her life had been chosen for rupture.

The apartment she had rented in Grey Lynn was small, with a single bedroom and a living area that faced the street. Within the first year after the bombing, she had stopped using the bedroom entirely. The small, enclosed space triggered a panic she could not override-a certainty that she had no options, that she was trapped. She began sleeping on the couch in the living room, where she could see the window and the street beyond it. The bedroom door remained closed. She had not opened it in over five years. Her career as a dancer had contracted around her fear in ways both obvious and subtle. She could no longer audition for roles that required her to perform in smaller venues or enclosed theatres. The idea of being backstage in a confined green room, waiting to go on, was impossible. She had begun to take only outdoor performances, which severely limited her opportunities in a city where most professional dance work happened in studios and theatre spaces. Her income had declined from what it had been before the bombing-she was making perhaps half of what she once earned, and the trajectory seemed to be downward. More significantly, she had begun to isolate herself from the dance community that had once been her entire world. Gatherings of dancers, conversations about upcoming shows, even casual mentions of the names of dancers she had once trained alongside-all of these had become unbearable because they threatened to pull her back into the life she had been building before the bombing, and that life now felt like it belonged to someone else.

When a stranger approached her on the street to ask for directions, Aroha felt her body prepare for violence. When a door closed unexpectedly in her apartment building, she found herself holding her breath, listening intently for footsteps, for the sound of someone entering her home. She had come to believe that nothing in her life held meaning anymore. The dance that had once brought her joy felt hollow. Her relationships had withered as she withdrew. She spent considerable energy trying to reframe what had happened to her in positive terms-telling herself that she had survived, that she was stronger now, that the experience had changed her in ways that might eventually matter-but these thoughts felt like mantras she was forcing herself to repeat rather than truths she believed. What haunted her most was the absence of accountability. The people responsible for the bombing had never been caught. They had never faced trial. They existed somewhere beyond her reach, unpunished, while she remained imprisoned by what they had done. She had come to therapy now because the isolation had become total, and because she was beginning to wonder whether the person she had been before the bombing-confident, ambitious, embedded in a community of artists-was someone she could ever become again, or whether she was going to spend the rest of her life as this fragmented version of herself, waiting for a sound that might never come.

Petra's Diminishment

Petra was sixty years old when she came to her first therapy appointment, though she moved through the waiting room as though carrying an invisible weight that had aged her beyond her years. She had worked as a midwife for thirty-seven years-the last fifteen at a teaching hospital in the Midwest where she had trained younger nurses and taken pride in her steady hands and the way families remembered her presence at their children's births. That Petra felt like someone else's story now.

The exposure had happened eighteen months earlier during a routine equipment maintenance shift. A chemical sterilant used to clean surgical instruments had leaked from a corroded valve in the supply room where Petra was inventorying stock. She had not seen the leak itself, but she had felt the burn in her throat and lungs almost immediately, a sensation like breathing fire. Her eyes watered so violently she could barely see. She had stumbled out into the hallway, gasping, and colleagues had rushed her to the emergency department. The hospital's occupational health team confirmed exposure to glutaraldehyde at levels that triggered a mandatory incident report. She had spent two days in the hospital being monitored, had been cleared medically within a week, and had returned to work after a month of light duty.

But something had fractured in those two days that medical clearance could not repair.

Within weeks, Petra had begun to notice that certain moments would send her into a state of acute panic. When she witnessed a patient bleeding during delivery-something that had once been simply part of her clinical reality, managed with practiced efficiency-she now found herself gripped by a terror so sudden and total that she had to step away from the bedside. The sight of blood triggered a cascade of physical sensations: her heart would race, her breathing would become shallow, and she would feel certain that something catastrophic was about to happen. She had come to believe that her body was fundamentally compromised, that exposure to that chemical had left her permanently fragile. What frightened her most was that she had no control over when these moments would arrive.

Over the following months, Petra had quietly begun to withdraw. She stopped volunteering for the busier shifts. When colleagues invited her to the regular Friday gatherings at the hospital café, she found reasons to decline-not because she did not want to go, but because maintaining those connections required her to explain or to risk judgment. She agreed to whatever schedule changes were proposed, whatever tasks were reassigned to her, because saying no felt dangerous, as though disagreement itself might trigger another crisis. Her partner, Maria, had noticed the change first: Petra no longer spoke about her work with the enthusiasm that had once animated their evenings. When Maria suggested they plan a trip-something they had always done each spring-Petra had felt a suffocating dread at the thought of committing to a future date, a future version of herself that she could not guarantee would be stable.

The feeling that nothing held meaning anymore had crept in gradually, like a slow leak. Delivering babies-the thing that had once felt like sacred work-now felt hollow. She would stand at the bedside of a laboring woman and feel nothing of the wonder she had once known. She had begun to think of herself as weak, as someone whose body had betrayed her and whose mind could no longer be trusted. The Petra who had trained residents and been called to the hardest deliveries seemed to have vanished, replaced by someone anxious and diminished.

What had finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis but a accumulation of small surrenders. She had requested a transfer to administrative duties, away from direct patient care. Maria had gently suggested that perhaps talking to someone might help. Petra had resisted for months-the thought of discussing the trauma, of reliving it in any form, had felt unbearable-but the weight of her own absence from her own life had become too much to carry alone. She sat in the therapy office now with her hands folded in her lap, uncertain whether she could be helped, uncertain whether the person she had been before the exposure could ever be found again.
